---
title: "About the project"
description: "Why errors in AI-driven scientific modeling can be productive, and how this Sloan Foundation project studies them: research questions, approach and milestones."
---

## Why study error?

AI is changing science, and AI models often get things wrong: they produce
biased results, fail on data unlike what they were trained on, break known
physical laws, and crash in ways their developers didn't expect. The usual
response is to remove the error as fast as possible.

But when scientists take an error seriously, they often learn something they
would not have learned otherwise. One AI weather model, FourCastNet, made
fast, skillful short-range forecasts, but a numerical instability kept it to
forecasts shorter than ten days. Researchers traced the problem to one
component: a Fourier transform that treats the globe as a flat sheet that wraps
around at the edges. Rebuilt with spherical harmonics, the model stayed stable
for a full simulated year ([Pathak et al. 2022; Bonev et al. 2023;
O'Loughlin et al. 2025](#references)). The error showed what the model needed
to respect. By diagnosing it, the team also showed they understood a system
that is otherwise hard to see inside.

Our question: **how can errors, and the ways scientists deal with them, make
AI-driven science better?**

## Goal

To develop a conceptual framework for understanding error as a productive and
generative feature of AI-driven scientific modeling, with a focus on climate
and Earth system science.

## Research questions

In plain terms, we are asking three things:

1. **Understanding.** What do scientists learn when an AI-driven model goes
   wrong, and does tracking down the error help explain how the model works?
2. **Antifragility.** Some systems gain from shocks rather than just surviving
   them ([Taleb 2012](#references)). When do models and modeling teams come
   out of a failure stronger, not just repaired?
3. **Credibility.** How do errors, and the way teams record, share and fix
   them, affect how far a model is trusted and how the teams themselves are
   organized?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## The research questions as worded in the proposal

1. How do errors in AI-driven models contribute to or constrain scientific
   understanding, and what do practices of error diagnosis reveal about model
   explainability?
2. In what ways do modeling communities develop antifragile responses to error,
   using failures to strengthen rather than merely repair their systems?
3. How do errors and their management shape the credibility of AI-driven models
   and the social organization of modeling teams?
:::

## Approach

- **Interviews** with scientists, software engineers and data specialists who
  work with AI-driven models at NSF NCAR, the LEAP Center (Learning the Earth
  with Artificial Intelligence and Physics) and NASA GISS.
- **Document analysis** of how errors are recorded: technical reports, code
  repositories, issue trackers and dataset documentation.
- **Philosophical analysis** that brings these findings together with work in
  philosophy of science and science and technology studies (STS).
- **An interdisciplinary [workshop](workshop.qmd)** where the developing
  framework is presented for feedback.
- **Talks** at the Philosophy of Science Association (PSA), the Society for
  Social Studies of Science (4S) and the American Geophysical Union (AGU).

## Why climate and Earth system science?

Climate scientists are adopting AI quickly while insisting that models respect
physical laws. Future climates lie outside the data any model was trained on,
so the reliability of AI models has direct stakes for society. The field also
has decades of shared model evaluation and data sharing to build on. We aim
for a framework that carries over to other sciences where AI is raising the
same questions.

## Milestones

- **October 1, 2026:** Project begins.
- **February 2027:** Call for extended abstracts and invitations to workshop
  speakers.
- **End of the first project year (date to be announced):**
  Interdisciplinary workshop.
- **September 30, 2028:** Project ends.

## Expected outcomes

- A recognized conceptual framework for error as a productive feature of
  AI-driven scientific modeling.
- A network connecting philosophers, STS scholars and scientists around this
  theme.
- Demonstrated relevance to scientific practice.

This project is supported by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation
(October 1, 2026 – September 30, 2028).
